paragraph_changes.before: ABSTRACT Genus-level identification of Paleocene–Eocene benthic foraminifera in thin section relies on expert morphological interpretation. This study presents a decision-support ontology with 21 controlled characters, 108 substantive states, and 706 graded rules for 75 genera. A deterministic engine ranks candidates from character observations, treats unobservable characters as neutral, and reports one of five evidence states. A decision-tree walk shares the knowledge base, and an optional vision-language layer drafts observations from images. Across 104 internal decision paths, the engine ranked the leaf genus uniquely first in 24 and jointly first in 10. It excluded the leaf in 17 paths, including 13 porcelaneous paths. The exploratory image-panel evaluation used one model pass per panel across 150 published panels covering 24 genera. Tie-aware top-1 agreement was 1.8% for 28 additional-article panels and 5.6% for 122 panels from a knowledge-base reference book. Replaying the same outputs while retaining raw uncertainty increased top-1 agreement from 4.9% to 8.9% overall, while rule-based reference exclusion remained at 45.3%. The pooled change in agreement is descriptive because the cohorts differ in scope and the book overlaps the knowledge base. The results characterize the prototype’s behavior on source-labeled material and motivate independent evaluation with expert character sheets.
paragraph_changes.after: ABSTRACT  Genus-level identification of Paleocene-Eocene benthic foraminifera in thin section requires morphological interpretation. We present an ontology with 21 controlled characters, 108 substantive states, 706 evidence-graded rules and 75 genera. An auditable engine ranks candidates while treating unobservable characters as neutral. A reproducible encoding revision removed 17 positive/contradictory overlaps, 10 mandatory/diagnostic conflicts and 25 repeated-scoring pairs. Across 104 unchanged internal decision paths, unique first ranks increased from 24 to 30, shared-rank top-three retrieval from 64 to 68, while excluded leaves increased from 17 to 19. The corrected engine achieved 3.2% tie-aware top-one agreement on 150 published image panels and 3.9% when raw uncertainty was retained; 122 panels overlap a knowledge-base reference book. Thirty-three weight/threshold configurations and a paired synthetic comparison against an unweighted eliminative key were evaluated offline. With 5% noise and 10%, 30% and 50% masking, synthetic top-one agreement was 62.4%, 43.7%, 22.6%. Three OWL cardinality restrictions and core-class disjointness were implemented and tested with HermiT. These development and synthetic tests characterize robustness under specified assumptions; the low image-panel agreement and remaining vocabulary gaps require independent validation.

paragraph_changes.before: The contributions of this article are: (1) a formal genus-level identification ontology for Paleocene–Eocene benthic foraminifera, built on 21 controlled characters with 108 character states and organized into three wall-composition modules of 25 genera each; (2) a deterministic inference framework in which each genus is represented by rule cards graded by evidence level (706 rules) and an observation set is mapped onto one of five graded confidence states, formalized in equations and pseudocode; (3) an evaluation logic in which unobservable characters are never equated with absence, so that the engine works with the incomplete observations typical of thin sections; (4) the linkage of the output to current taxonomic validity (WoRMS) and to paleoenvironmental records; (5) an open-access implementation of the knowledge base as a Web application backed by a graph database; and (6) an evaluation comprising an internal consistency test over all decision paths, a knowledge-base integrity audit, seven counterfactual ablations, and an exploratory, source-labeled image-panel case series with cluster-bootstrap intervals, reported together with its limitations; the planned blinded multi-expert evaluation is specified as future work.
paragraph_changes.after: The contributions of this article are: (1) a formal genus-level identification ontology for Paleocene–Eocene benthic foraminifera, built on 21 controlled characters with 108 character states and organized into three wall-composition modules of 25 genera each; (2) a deterministic inference framework in which each genus is represented by rule cards graded by evidence level (706 rules) and an observation set is mapped onto one of five graded confidence states, formalized in equations and pseudocode; (3) an evaluation logic in which unobservable characters are never equated with absence, so that the engine works with the incomplete observations typical of thin sections; (4) the linkage of the output to current taxonomic validity (WoRMS) and to paleoenvironmental records; (5) an open-access implementation of the knowledge base as a Web application backed by a graph database; and (6) an evaluation comprising an internal consistency test over all decision paths, a knowledge-base integrity audit, seven counterfactual ablations, completed weight/threshold sensitivity, a paired synthetic eliminative-key baseline, and an exploratory, source-labeled image-panel case series with cluster-bootstrap intervals, reported together with its limitations; the planned blinded multi-expert evaluation is specified as future work.

paragraph_changes.before: OWL structure: The ontology (file foram_ontology_v1.owl, Supplementary Material S3) is a lightweight OWL 2 schema with a large assertional component (Supplementary Table S9.6). Its nine classes are Genus, Module, MorphologicalCharacter, CharacterValue, RuleItem, DecisionQuestion, DecisionOutcome, ObservationState, and IdentificationStatus; runtime observations are not persisted. Genera are linked to modules (belongsToModule) and to rule items through hasRule and its four sub-properties hasMandatoryRule, hasDiagnosticRule, hasSupportingRule, and hasContradictoryRule; rule items reference characters (refersToCharacter) with the expected state and mapping confidence as data values; characters list their permitted states (allowedValue); and decision questions are linked to characters (asksAboutCharacter), to the next question, and to genera (leadsToGenus). Fig. 2 shows the schema. Because rules are represented as individuals, identification is computed by the scoring engine rather than by a description-logic reasoner. The current axioms are limited to property hierarchies, domain and range restrictions, and functional datatype properties (DL expressivity ALH(D)). The next release adds constraining axioms such as:
paragraph_changes.after: OWL structure: The lightweight OWL 2 ontology contains nine classes: Genus, Module, MorphologicalCharacter, CharacterValue, RuleItem, DecisionQuestion, DecisionOutcome, ObservationState and IdentificationStatus. The existing property hierarchies, domain/range axioms and functional datatype properties are retained. The export now includes three qualified cardinality restrictions and an AllDisjointClasses axiom for the six core entity types, as specified below. Module and controlled-value individuals are explicitly distinguished with two AllDifferent axioms. The generated inventory is reported in Supplementary Material S10; identification still uses the rule scorer rather than a description-logic reasoner. eval/generate_ontology.py regenerates the constraints and synchronizes current rule mappings on every export.

paragraph_changes.before: Reasoning and pitfall scanning: The ontology was classified with HermiT [47] in Protégé [48] and is consistent with no unsatisfiable classes. Because it contains no disjointness axioms, consistency is a weak guarantee; the disjointness axioms above are therefore planned for the next release so that the reasoner can detect category errors. The OOPS! pitfall scanner [49] has not been applied to this version; structural quality was instead evaluated directly through the automated knowledge-base integrity audit described below.
paragraph_changes.after: Reasoning and pitfall scanning: The revised OWL file was classified using HermiT [47] through Owlready2 and was consistent with no unsatisfiable named classes. Four isolated negative controls were rejected: an individual typed as both Genus and RuleItem, a genus assigned to two explicitly distinct modules, an evidenceLevel value outside the four-value enumeration, and a character constrained to at most one allowed value in conflict with the minimum of two. These are actual reasoner runs, not inferred results. Three class restrictions, one n-ary disjointness axiom (15 pairwise class relations) and two AllDifferent axioms are counted separately. Closed-world JSON checks additionally verify the asserted cardinalities; OWL open-world semantics do not make a missing assertion an automatic validation failure. OOPS! [49] was not run.

paragraph_changes.before: Knowledge-base integrity audit: Consistency of the OWL file does not guarantee that the rule cards are free of domain errors, so the knowledge base is also checked by an automated audit that reports: (a) contradictory rules whose character–state pair equals a positive rule of the same genus; (b) mandatory rules that conflict with another mandatory or diagnostic rule on the same character; (c) rules whose text is negated but whose mapping is positive (polarity errors); (d) character–state pairs counted more than once within one genus (by two diagnostic or supporting rules, or by a mandatory and a diagnostic rule); (e) mandatory rules without a mapping; (f) genera without a scoring diagnostic rule; (g) decision-tree answers outside the controlled vocabulary; (h) characters queried again along one decision path; and (i) genera not assigned to exactly one module. A first run of the audit identified 13 mapping errors, ten inverted polarities, and three pairs mapped to the wrong character or combined with an unintended second pair, which were corrected. After this correction the audit reports 17 rules in (a), 10 conflicting rule pairs in (b), 4 rules flagged in (c), none of them an inverted mapping on inspection, 25 multiply counted pairs in (d), 27 rules in (e), 18 genera in (f), 7 answers in (g), five of which are resolved by an explicit mapping to another character, 11 nodes in (h), and none in (i). These counts were reproduced on the evaluated version (base commit 1e12fb5) and are listed item by item in Supplementary Material S1. They remain unresolved and are the input of the rule-card revision and of the planned expert review (Section VIII-B); the audit is implemented in eval/audit.py.
paragraph_changes.after: Knowledge-base integrity audit: The audit checks (a) positive/contradictory pair overlap, (b) conflicting mandatory/diagnostic mappings, (c) a lexical negation screen, (d) repeated scored pairs, (e) unmapped mandatory rules, (f) genera without a scored diagnostic, (g) out-of-vocabulary tree answers, (h) repeated questions and (i) module cardinality. The immutable pre-revision master reproduced 17/10/25 findings in (a)/(b)/(d). Sixty-seven documented encoding edits reduced all three to zero without changing reference labels, tree answers, evidence grades or the 706 original rule statements. Scope errors were removed, ontogenetic transitions were encoded explicitly, redundant scoring pairs were retired, and statements not expressible in the vocabulary were retained as non-scoring hints. Of the original 18 genera without a scored diagnostic, three received a literal or existing-tree-supported mapping; 15 could not be completed without inventing anatomy or extending the vocabulary. Retiring false diagnostic proxies leaves 28 genera without a scored diagnostic overall. Remaining counts are (c) 3 lexical flags, (e) 28 unmapped mandatory rules, (f) 28 genera, (g) 7 answers, (h) 11 nodes and (i) 0 genera. These findings and the full before/after ledger are supplied in Supplementary Material S10. The repairs are encoding consistency work, not independent taxonomic validation.

paragraph_changes.before: We evaluated internal agreement across decision-tree paths (Section VIII-A), explored agreement with published image-panel labels (Sections VIII-C, VIII-D, and VIII-F), and ran seven scoring counterfactuals and a paired normalization replay (Sections VIII-E and VIII-G). Section VIII-B describes the planned independent expert study. The supplementary package contains the archived inputs, raw outputs, and replay scripts.
paragraph_changes.after: We evaluated unchanged internal paths (VIII-A), replayed 150 archived VLM observation sheets (VIII-C–D and VIII-F–G), ran seven ablations and 33 weight/threshold configurations (VIII-E), and compared the scorer with an unweighted eliminative key in a paired synthetic stress test (VIII-H). VIII-B retains the future independent expert protocol. No expert observations, new VLM calls, hidden test-set tuning or simulated human assessments are claimed. S1–S9 describe the frozen earlier evaluation; S10 contains the corrected masters, current outputs, before/after comparisons and reproduction scripts.

paragraph_changes.before: Counts of paths; ties share the rank. CONF. = CONFIRMED_GENUS outputs whose top genus is (correct) or is not (incorrect) the leaf genus. Values recomputed on the evaluated version (base commit 1e12fb5), after the correction of 13 mappings and without any external expert review of the rule cards; they are reproduced by api/test/consistency.test.js and listed per path in Supplementary Material S6. These are shared-rank retrieval counts, not the tie-fractional, abstention-aware agreement of Section VIII-D.
paragraph_changes.after: Counts use shared score ranks and do not count abstentions as retrieved identifications. The same 104 path observations and leaf labels were retained. The current JavaScript engine and independent Python Engine M agree on every path state and displayed output. Unique first ranks increased from 24 to 30 and shared-rank top-three retrieval from 64 to 68; excluded leaves increased from 17 to 19. Fractional, abstention-aware Acc@1/Acc@3 changed from 20.0%/46.0% to 25.1%/46.7%. Thus removing audit findings did not resolve all tree–rule disagreements. Original results remain frozen, and current path-level triggers are in S10.

paragraph_changes.before: An offline replay reproduced the 104 frozen paths and identified the exclusion triggers. Sixteen paths violated mandatory rules. One path to Vertebralina triggered a strong contradiction with score −2 and no mandatory violation. On eight of the 13 porcelaneous exclusions, the tree supplied CHR_10 = SIMPLE and a mandatory rule expected SUBDIVIDED. Masking CHR_10 = SIMPLE wherever it occurred in the 25 affected porcelaneous paths reduced exclusions from 13 to six across all 42 paths in that module. Tie-aware top-1 and top-3 agreement decreased from 15.9% to 9.5% and from 40.9% to 27.8%, respectively. This perturbation localizes a disagreement and leaves the evaluated tree and rule base intact. Supplementary Material S9 gives the path-level traces.
paragraph_changes.after: The revised path replay records 19 excluded leaves and the exact responsible rule statements. A CSV defect in the earlier evaluation script was also corrected: the generic leaf_excluded column had been populated from historical Engine R while the reported results used Engine M. The current export labels both engines separately and supplies Engine M exclusion triggers consistently. No path answer was masked, relabeled or removed to increase agreement. Composite questions still carry information outside the controlled vocabulary, and internal retrieval remains a development consistency measure.

paragraph_changes.before: For the normalization sensitivity analysis, we reproduced the archived outputs from all 150 raw responses with the frozen controller, rule mappings, and scorer. In a paired replay we restored the raw UNCERTAIN or NOT_OBSERVABLE state for the 184 entries promoted to an evaluable state, retaining other preprocessing. The scorer ignores values in a neutral state. We re-inferred the module from CHR_01, without reference labels, and scored each replay locally. paragraph_changes.after: Normalization replay: The original provider receipts and application-normalized sheets were retained. In a paired secondary replay, only raw UNCERTAIN or NOT_OBSERVABLE entries promoted to an evaluable state were restored to neutrality; all other normalization was retained. Module selection was re-inferred from CHR_01 without reference labels. Both conditions use the corrected master. Descriptive percentile intervals use 2,000 paired resamples of source/section clusters (seed 20261111); S10 also supplies the frozen pre-curation replay for comparison.

paragraph_changes.after: E. Ablation, Weight and Threshold Sensitivity Analyses

paragraph_changes.before: Seven prespecified counterfactuals (Table X) remove or modify one mechanism at a time. A1 sets every rule group that refers to an unobserved character to MISMATCH; this operationalizes “unobservable treated as absent” without claiming that ABSENT is a valid state of every character, and n(O) remains the actual number of observed characters. A2 removes the 13 implication mappings; A3 removes the contradictory rules; A4 makes multi-pair rules strictly conjunctive (MATCH only if every mapped character group is observed and holds, an observed mismatch still taking precedence); A5 evaluates the tie test (line 11 of Algorithm 1) after the PROBABLE test (line 12); A6 additionally requires a margin Δ ≥ wM = 3 for the PROBABLE test, a missing runner-up counting as an infinite margin; and A7 divides S(g|O) by the total positive weight of the rules of g whose verdict is not NEUTRAL. A7 keeps the released confidence thresholds, whose scale no longer matches the normalized scores, so that it yields no CONFIRMED_GENUS output. The counterfactuals were evaluated on the 104 internal decision-tree paths of Section VIII-A and on the 150 VLM-derived observation sheets of Section VIII-C (Supplementary Material S6); they were not evaluated on expert character sheets, which do not exist.
paragraph_changes.after: Seven prespecified counterfactuals (Table X) remove or modify one mechanism at a time. A1 sets every rule group that refers to an unobserved character to  MISMATCH ; this operationalizes “unobservable treated as absent” without claiming that  ABSENT  is a valid state of every character, and n(O) remains the actual number of observed characters. A2 removes the 13 implication mappings; A3 removes the contradictory rules; A4 makes multi-pair rules strictly conjunctive ( MATCH  only if every mapped character group is observed and holds, an observed mismatch still taking precedence); A5 evaluates the tie test (line 11 of Algorithm 1) after the PROBABLE test (line 12); A6 additionally requires a margin Δ  ≥  w M  = 3 for the PROBABLE test, a missing runner-up counting as an infinite margin; and A7 divides S(g|O) by the total positive weight of the rules of g whose verdict is not  NEUTRAL . A7 keeps the released confidence thresholds, whose scale no longer matches the normalized scores, so that it yields no  CONFIRMED_GENUS  output. The counterfactuals were rerun with the corrected master on the 104 internal decision-tree paths of Section VIII-A and on the 150 VLM-derived observation sheets of Section VIII-C (Supplementary Material S6); they were not evaluated on expert character sheets, which do not exist.

paragraph_changes.before: On the internal paths, A1 had by far the largest effect: the leaf genus was excluded in 82.7% of the paths instead of 16.3%, and tie-aware Acc@3 fell from 46.0% to 12.8%, which shows that treating unobservable characters as absent would defeat the neutral-evidence mechanism. A7 reduced Acc@1 and Acc@3 to 10.4% and 26.2%, A2–A4 changed Acc@1 by less than one percentage point, and A5 and A6 left all path results unchanged. On the VLM-derived sheets, every configuration remained at low agreement (Acc@1 1.8%–6.2%, Acc@3 12.1%–20.7%), and A1 changed the results only slightly (Acc@1 6.2%, Acc@3 18.3%), consistent with the small fraction of characters that were unobservable after normalization (Supplementary Fig. S9.12). These contrasts are internal or VLM-based; they are not estimates of accuracy on expert observations.
paragraph_changes.after: With the corrected master, A1 produced 81.7% excluded leaves and Acc@1/Acc@3 of 9.4%/14.2%, compared with 18.3% and 25.1%/46.7% for A0. All ablations were computed on the same observations and use the current master (Table X). Supporting tables distinguish the frozen pre-curation results from these replays. These contrasts characterize internal and VLM-derived inputs, not expert accuracy.

paragraph_changes.before: Planned weight sensitivity. The effect of the evidence weights and thresholds remains to be quantified. A future analysis will vary the weights and thresholds and summarize ranking stability with rank-biased overlap [69].
paragraph_changes.after: Completed weight/threshold sensitivity: eval/sensitivity.py evaluated A0, equal weights (+1,+1,+1,−1), mandatory-dominant weights (+5,+3,+1,−5), no supporting score (+3,+5,0,−5), contradiction penalties −3 and −10, and all 27 combinations of τ_obs ∈ {1,2,3}, τ_NM ∈ {2,3,4}, δ ∈ {1,2,3}. These 33 configurations were applied to the 104 frozen paths and 150 archived VLM sheets; state-preserving panel replays are supplied separately. Rank-biased overlap [69] uses p=0.9 and the finite unequal-list extrapolation (Eq. 32), with the actual deterministic tie order; accuracy retains fractional score ties. Top-1 and top-3 stability are agreement with A0, separately from agreement with the reference genus. Table XII reports all five weight alternatives. Threshold variation left every ranking unchanged (RBO and top-1/top-3 stability = 1.0), while path Acc@1 ranged from 21.3% to 25.1% through altered abstention; panel Acc@1 remained 3.2%. No configuration was selected as an optimum, and these are development analyses rather than a held-out tuning result.

paragraph_changes.before: Table XI summarizes the agreement of the VLM and engine pipeline with the published genus labels. For the 28 additional-article panels, Acc@1 was 1.8% (95% cluster-bootstrap interval 0.0%–4.0%) and Acc@3 46.4% (0.0%–68.6%); for the 122 panels from the knowledge-base reference book, Acc@1 was 5.6% (2.4%–8.8%) and Acc@3 14.1% (7.0%–22.3%). The pooled, imbalanced 150-panel set had Acc@1 = 4.9% (2.1%–7.6%) and Acc@3 = 20.1% (10.2%–31.2%); these pooled values are descriptive and do not constitute independent external validation. Coverage was 88.7% (81.3%–94.5%), and the published reference genus was excluded in 45.3% (34.2%–56.7%) of the panels. The comparatively high Acc@3 of the additional-article cohort rests on two genera and nine clusters, as its wide interval shows. Complete panel-level outputs and source-stratified estimates are given in Supplementary Materials S7 and S8.
paragraph_changes.after: Table XI reports the corrected-master replay against published labels. additional-article panels: Acc@1 3.6 [0.0-5.1]%, Acc@3 14.3 [0.0-20.5]%; reference-book panels: Acc@1 3.1 [0.8-5.9]%, Acc@3 10.8 [5.6-16.4]%. Pooled Acc@1/Acc@3 were 3.2%/11.4%, versus 4.9%/20.1% with the frozen pre-curation master on the same normalized sheets. Rule-based reference exclusion was 44.7%. Encoding repairs improved some internal rankings while reducing image-panel agreement; this adverse result is retained. The 122 book panels remain source-overlapping and the pooled values remain descriptive.

paragraph_changes.before: After normalization, every panel had φ < 0.4 (Supplementary Fig. S9.12). The upper missingness bins contained few panels and have wide intervals. All 68 observed rule-based reference exclusions in the released panel replay were attributed to mandatory rule conflicts. A further 43 references fell outside the module selected from CHR_01. The present design cannot attribute these disagreements separately to visual observation errors, reference labels, or the rules.
paragraph_changes.after: The normalized observation sheets and missingness fractions were not regenerated. With the corrected master, 67 published reference genera were eliminated by rules and 43 were omitted through the module selected from CHR_01. These are distinct causes of absence from the candidate ranking. The design cannot assign the disagreements uniquely to visual observation errors, published labels or knowledge-base validity. Frozen S9 figures describe the earlier master; current statistics and plots are supplied in S10.

paragraph_changes.after: Errors remained systematic. The most frequently displayed genus in the corrected pooled replay was Ranikothalia (36 panels). The displayed first name and fractional score-tie credit are distinct outcomes, and complete per-panel ranks and omissions are retained. No poorly performing panel was removed after curation.

paragraph_changes.before: Confidence-state agreement varied across the two cohorts (Fig. 3). In the book cohort, CONFIRMED_GENUS occurred in 64 of 122 panels and achieved 1.6% top-1 agreement (95% cluster interval 0.0%–5.4%). In the additional articles it occurred in 10 of 28 panels with 0.0% agreement. CANDIDATE_GENUS achieved 14.2% in the book and 2.9% in the articles. On the internal paths, 14 of 48 CONFIRMED_GENUS outputs identified the leaf (Table VIII). The rule-defined states should be interpreted with their underlying evidence and evaluated separately on independent expert inputs.
paragraph_changes.after: Confidence-state agreement remains low (Fig. 3, regenerated for the corrected master). CONFIRMED_GENUS occurred in 79 panels, with 1.3% mean fractional top-one agreement. On internal paths, 17 of 29 confirmed outputs named the leaf (Table VIII). These categories describe rule evidence and should not be interpreted as calibrated probabilities of correctness.

paragraph_changes.before: All ten competency queries matched their master-JSON answers. The archived API run passed 43 tests, including the worked scoring example (Table VII) and internal paths (Table VIII). Supplementary Material S9 includes the test summary and the new path replay.
paragraph_changes.after: The pre-curation archive records ten read-only competency-query matches. The revised local API suite passes 47 tests, including the worked example, every internal path state/output and configurable thresholds. Seven additional scientific tests check RBO properties, tie credit, frozen image hashes, audit targets, paired masking/noise, ranking invariance under threshold changes and preservation of the default scoring algorithm. HermiT and its negative controls are reported in Section IV-B and S10. Database synchronization, when performed, is recorded separately; no unverified live-deployment claim is made.

With the corrected master, pooled Acc@1 changed from 3.2% to 3.9% (paired difference 0.7 percentage points; 95% cluster interval 0.0 to 2.3). Acc@3 changed from 11.4% to 12.4%. The earlier 4.9%-to-8.9% replay is reproducible only with the frozen pre-curation master; it is retained as a historical comparison, not attributed to the corrected knowledge base.

paragraph_changes.before: Knowledge-base validity: The character and rule sets were extended from seven pilot taxa to 75 genera by a single-author literature synthesis, and per-rule bibliographic provenance is not yet recorded (Supplementary Material S1). The integrity audit reduces, but does not eliminate, the associated risk, and its remaining findings (Section IV-B) are unresolved; the planned expert review (Section VIII-B) has not yet been conducted, and a broader community review is planned.
paragraph_changes.after: Knowledge-base validity: Per-rule bibliographic pages and independent multi-expert validation remain unavailable. The revision removes specific encoding conflicts but cannot supply omitted anatomical concepts. Only three of the original 18 unmapped diagnostic genera could be completed from literal existing states or the development tree; 15 remain unresolved, and 28 genera overall have no scored diagnostic after retiring false proxies. Increasing a consistency score by labeling generic shared anatomy as diagnostic would overstate the knowledge base. Synthetic profiles and internal paths share the same rule source, so their results cannot establish taxonomic validity or external generalization.

paragraph_changes.before: The ontology describes 75 benthic foraminiferal genera using 21 controlled characters and 706 evidence-graded rules. The deterministic scorer traces its outputs to those rules, and a decision tree offers a second route. The internal path audit traced 17 exclusions to rule conflicts. In the 150-panel case series, preserving raw uncertainty raised pooled top-1 agreement from 4.9% to 8.9% while the rule-based exclusion rate held at 45.3%. The results identify normalization and tree–rule alignment as priorities for revision and independent evaluation.
paragraph_changes.after: The ontology encodes 75 genera, 21 controlled characters and 706 graded rule statements. Documented encoding repairs removed the three targeted audit categories, increased unique internal first ranks from 24 to 30 and shared-rank top-three retrieval from 64 to 68, but left 19 excluded paths and reduced image-panel agreement to 3.2%. Completed weight/threshold sensitivity and a paired eliminative-key stress test quantify behavior without requiring human observers. The synthetic comparison favors graded scoring under the specified masking/noise process; it does not remedy low agreement on published images. Three cardinality restrictions and core-class disjointness were implemented and passed actual reasoner and negative-control checks.

paragraph_changes.before: The prototype supports specialist review of the morphological evidence behind each ranking. Priorities include blinded multi-institutional testing with experts, a multi-access key baseline, weight and threshold sensitivity analysis, curation of per-rule sources and taxonomic authorities, and review of the flagged rule cards. Further development includes adding genera and stratigraphic intervals, testing thin-section image models and usability, and combining differently oriented sections of the same specimen.
paragraph_changes.after: Priorities are independent source-disjoint evaluation, anatomical vocabulary extensions, taxonomic and per-rule source curation, reconciliation of the remaining tree–rule conflicts, and calibration of confidence states. The multi-access comparator and weight/threshold analysis are now completed development experiments, rather than promised future experiments. Expert validation remains future work; no numerical reviewer score or acceptance probability follows from these revisions.
